title: Pulmonary Function Testing: Pattern, Quality, and Clinical Correlation
bottomLine: Pulmonary function tests describe physiology; they do not diagnose disease by themselves. First confirm test quality, then identify obstruction, restriction or diffusion impairment, assess bronchodilator response where relevant, and interpret the pattern against symptoms, exposures and imaging.
recognize: A reduced FEV1/FVC supports airflow obstruction when interpreted against an appropriate lower limit of normal rather than a rigid one-size cutoff in every patient.
A low FVC can reflect restriction, air trapping or suboptimal effort; true restriction requires reduced lung volumes, not spirometry alone.
DLCO can fall with emphysema, ILD, pulmonary vascular disease or anemia and therefore requires context.
differentiate: Obstruction with reversibility/variability can support asthma physiology, but absence of a large single bronchodilator response does not exclude asthma.
Restriction on spirometry is only suspected until lung-volume testing confirms reduced total lung capacity.
Do not infer race-based biologic correction; interpret using current equitable reference standards and the patient's clinical context.
assessment: Confirm indication, symptom pattern, smoking/vaping/occupational exposure, inhaler timing, recent infection and ability to perform acceptable manoeuvres.
Review whether the report met quality/reproducibility criteria before acting on borderline values.
workup: Use spirometry, bronchodilator testing, lung volumes and diffusion capacity selectively according to the diagnostic question.
Pair unexpected restriction/diffusion impairment with imaging, hemoglobin and cardiopulmonary evaluation when appropriate.
management: Treat the disease pattern only after clinical correlation; use spirometry to support diagnosis, stage physiologic impairment and monitor change when that will alter care.
Refer to respirology for unexplained mixed physiology, progressive restriction/DLCO decline, severe obstruction, discordant symptoms or uncertain test quality.
medicationSafety: Do not escalate inhaled therapy solely because FEV1 is low without confirming diagnosis, symptoms, exacerbation history and technique/adherence.
Medication withholding before testing depends on the purpose of the study and laboratory instructions.
redFlags: Disproportionately low DLCO with pulmonary vascular concern
counselling: Explain that PFTs measure how the lungs move and exchange gas rather than naming the disease on their own.
followUp: Repeat testing only when the trend can change diagnosis, treatment or prognosis; close the loop on abnormal studies requiring imaging or specialist review.
examTrap: Calling low FVC 'restrictive lung disease' without confirming total lung capacity—or diagnosing COPD from one ratio without quality/context.
oneLinePearl: Read PFTs in three steps: quality, pattern, clinical context.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current Pulmonary Function Testing resources, including 2023 interpretation equity guidance

title: Oxygen Therapy: Treat Hypoxemia, Prescribe the Target and Reassess
bottomLine: Oxygen is a medication for hypoxemia, not breathlessness itself. Prescribe a target saturation/range appropriate to the clinical context, use the lowest effective delivery strategy, reassess after changes, and distinguish acute oxygen support from long-term oxygen qualification.
recognize: Dyspnea with normal oxygenation does not automatically improve with supplemental oxygen and requires diagnosis-directed care.
Patients at risk of chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure may need a controlled oxygen target rather than unrestricted high-flow oxygen.
Long-term oxygen therapy is a chronic hypoxemia intervention and uses stable-state criteria rather than a single acute-illness saturation.
differentiate: Acute hypoxemia during pneumonia/COPD/HF is different from chronic stable resting hypoxemia qualifying for home oxygen.
Oxygen treats arterial hypoxemia; it does not correct tissue hypoperfusion from shock if circulation is inadequate.
assessment: Assess saturation, respiratory effort, mental status, hemodynamics, underlying disease, baseline oxygen use and hypercapnia risk.
For chronic prescribing, confirm the patient is clinically stable enough for qualification testing and address smoking/fire risk.
workup: Use pulse oximetry for monitoring and blood gas when hypercapnia, severe respiratory failure or uncertainty about ventilation matters.
Long-term oxygen eligibility should follow current Canadian/provincial program criteria and validated assessment rather than an outpatient guess from one reading.
management: In acute hypoxemia, titrate oxygen to the prescribed clinical target while treating the underlying cause.
If escalating oxygen requirement persists, reassess for pneumonia, edema, PE, pneumothorax, mucus plugging or ventilatory failure rather than only increasing the device.
Home oxygen requires a documented indication, device/flow plan, safety education and reassessment after transient illness when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Uncontrolled oxygen can worsen CO2 retention in susceptible patients; monitor clinical status and blood gas when hypercapnic failure is plausible.
Oxygen is a combustion hazard; smoking/open flame around home oxygen is dangerous.
redFlags: Altered mental status or hypercapnic concern
counselling: Teach the prescribed flow/device and fire safety; patients should not self-increase long-term oxygen indefinitely without reassessment.
Explain that oxygen and inhalers treat different physiologic problems.
followUp: Reassess oxygen requirement after acute illness and verify ongoing home-oxygen need according to local program standards.
Track functional response and equipment adherence/safety.
examTrap: Giving oxygen for anxiety-related dyspnea with normal saturation—or writing permanent home oxygen from one low saturation during an acute infection.
oneLinePearl: Oxygen needs an indication, a target, and a reassessment plan.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society COPD/home ventilation and oxygen-related guidance

title: Thoracentesis: Diagnose and Relieve Pleural Fluid Safely
bottomLine: Thoracentesis is performed to answer a pleural-fluid question, relieve significant symptoms, or both. Confirm that the result will change management, use image guidance and appropriate procedural expertise, and monitor for pneumothorax, bleeding, infection and re-expansion-related complications.
recognize: New unilateral, unexplained or clinically significant pleural effusion often warrants diagnostic evaluation unless the cause is already clear and responding as expected.
Large effusions can cause dyspnea/hypoxemia; infected pleural space may require drainage rather than repeated needle sampling alone.
differentiate: Heart-failure-associated bilateral effusions that improve with therapy may not need immediate sampling; atypical/asymmetric/nonresolving features change that decision.
Thoracentesis is not the definitive treatment for every recurrent malignant or infected effusion; chest tube, indwelling catheter or specialist intervention may be required.
assessment: Assess size/location by imaging, respiratory symptoms, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, bleeding risk, infection signs and whether the patient can safely cooperate/position.
Clarify whether the procedure is diagnostic, therapeutic or both and what tests are needed on the fluid.
workup: Use bedside ultrasound/image guidance for site selection whenever available and appropriate.
Pleural studies commonly include protein/LDH with paired serum values, cell count/differential, pH/glucose when infection is suspected, microbiology and cytology according to the differential.
management: Perform only within training/scope and local procedural governance, with sterile technique and monitoring.
Stop and reassess for chest pain, severe cough, dyspnea, hypotension or other concerning symptoms during drainage.
Postprocedure imaging is symptom/risk dependent rather than automatically required after every uncomplicated ultrasound-guided procedure.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation/antiplatelet decisions are individualized to bleeding risk, urgency and local procedural guidance; do not apply a universal hold interval to every drug/patient.
Avoid excessive local anesthetic dosing and maintain sterile procedural technique.
redFlags: Empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring definitive drainage
counselling: Explain whether the procedure is being done to identify the cause, relieve dyspnea or both, and discuss symptoms that require urgent reassessment afterward.
followUp: Track fluid results to a final diagnosis and ensure cytology/microbiology are closed-loop.
Recurrent or complicated effusions require specialty follow-up rather than serial isolated taps.
examTrap: Doing a thoracentesis simply because an effusion exists without asking what question the fluid will answer—or missing empyema that needs definitive drainage.
oneLinePearl: Before tapping pleural fluid, know the question and the next step after the answer.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society chest-procedure practice resources
Canadian pleural-procedure and Choosing Wisely principles

title: Pulmonary Nodule: Estimate Cancer Risk Before Ordering the Next Scan
bottomLine: An incidental pulmonary nodule is managed by malignancy probability, size/morphology, growth, patient risk and whether the patient could benefit from treatment. Compare prior imaging first, then choose surveillance, PET/CT, biopsy or specialty referral rather than repeating CTs indefinitely.
recognize: Risk rises with older age, smoking history, prior cancer, suspicious morphology, upper-lobe location and documented growth.
Many small nodules are benign and over-imaging can cause radiation, anxiety and invasive downstream harm.
differentiate: A nodule found during formal lung-cancer screening follows the screening program algorithm; an incidental nodule follows an incidental-nodule pathway.
Symptoms such as hemoptysis or weight loss move the patient from 'incidental surveillance' toward diagnostic evaluation.
assessment: Review exact nodule size, density (solid/subsolid), morphology, number, prior imaging/growth, smoking exposure, age, prior malignancy and treatment preferences/fitness.
Check whether the radiology report already recommends a validated follow-up pathway.
workup: Retrieve prior imaging before ordering another scan whenever possible.
Use a validated risk model or guideline framework when appropriate; PET/CT, biopsy and specialty referral are reserved for risk levels where they can change management.
management: Follow current Canadian/provincial lung-nodule/screening pathways and radiology recommendations rather than inventing one universal interval.
Refer moderate/high-risk, growing or technically concerning nodules for respirology/thoracic/oncology assessment.
Avoid surveillance in situations where the patient would not pursue or benefit from cancer treatment after shared decision-making.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary contrast or invasive biopsy when surveillance is the evidence-based next step; consider renal/allergy/bleeding risk for downstream procedures.
counselling: Explain absolute cancer risk and why 'watching' can be safer than immediate biopsy for low-risk nodules.
Use smoking-cessation support without blaming the patient for the finding.
followUp: Create a closed-loop recall system so surveillance imaging is not lost.
Document completion or handoff of nodule follow-up rather than leaving responsibility ambiguous.
examTrap: Ordering yearly CT forever for a stable low-risk nodule—or biopsying a tiny low-risk lesion before reviewing prior imaging.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary nodule care is risk-stratified surveillance, not reflex biopsy or endless scanning.
sourceBasis: Canadian lung cancer screening/provincial pulmonary nodule pathways
Canadian Thoracic Society/Choosing Wisely respiratory imaging principles

title: Interstitial Lung Disease: Recognize Restriction, Exposures, Autoimmune Clues, and Progression
bottomLine: Interstitial lung disease is a family of diffuse parenchymal disorders. Suspect it in persistent exertional dyspnea, dry cough, crackles, restriction or diffusion impairment; obtain exposure/medication/autoimmune history and appropriate HRCT/PFT assessment, then refer early because subtype and progression determine treatment.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, fine inspiratory crackles, clubbing, restrictive physiology and reduced diffusion capacity are common clues.
Connective-tissue disease, occupational/environmental exposures, medications, radiation and hypersensitivity exposures can drive ILD.
differentiate: Heart failure, COPD/emphysema, obesity, infection and pulmonary vascular disease can mimic ILD symptoms or coexist.
An acute ILD exacerbation is a different emergency from gradual chronic progression and requires hospital-level evaluation.
assessment: Take a detailed occupational, avocational, home/mould/bird, medication, smoking/vaping and autoimmune-system review.
Assess oxygenation at rest/exertion, functional decline, crackles, clubbing, edema and systemic rheumatologic features.
workup: Use high-resolution chest CT and complete PFTs including diffusion capacity to characterize suspected fibrotic ILD.
Order targeted autoimmune/exposure testing based on the clinical phenotype; multidisciplinary specialist review may be needed before labeling idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or another subtype.
Before immunosuppression, follow current CTS infection-screening guidance.
management: Remove harmful exposures when identified and provide smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation/oxygen assessment and comorbidity care as appropriate.
Antifibrotic or immunosuppressive therapy is subtype- and progression-specific and should be specialist coordinated.
Refer early for progressive disease, uncertain subtype, significant physiologic impairment or transplant/palliative-care consideration.
medicationSafety: Do not empirically start chronic systemic corticosteroids for undifferentiated fibrotic ILD; some fibrotic subtypes are not steroid-responsive and immunosuppression can be harmful.
Screen infection risk before significant immunosuppression according to current CTS guidance.
counselling: Explain that ILD treatment depends on the exact subtype and trend; a fibrosis label on CT is not the final diagnosis.
Discuss exposure avoidance and early specialty follow-up.
followUp: Trend symptoms, exercise oxygenation and PFTs at an interval appropriate to the subtype and severity.
Escalate when decline exceeds expected measurement variability or new complications emerge.
examTrap: Calling every restrictive PFT 'pulmonary fibrosis' and starting prednisone without HRCT/subtype evaluation.
oneLinePearl: ILD diagnosis is exposure + physiology + HRCT + multidisciplinary pattern recognition.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current ILD evaluation/monitoring standards
CTS 2026 Infection Screening Before Immunosuppression in ILD position statement

title: Occupational Lung Disease: Ask What Changes at Work and Away From Work
bottomLine: Occupational lung disease is diagnosed by linking exposure to a compatible physiologic or imaging pattern. Ask the job, task, agent, duration and whether symptoms/lung function improve away from exposure; early exposure control and objective documentation matter because continued exposure can cause irreversible disease.
recognize: Work-related asthma may worsen during shifts/work weeks and improve on weekends or holidays; latency can occur after sensitization.
Silica, asbestos, welding fumes, dusts, vapours and other agents can cause chronic airway disease, pneumoconiosis or ILD depending on exposure.
differentiate: Pre-existing asthma worsened by irritants is different from new sensitizer-induced occupational asthma, although both require exposure management.
A temporal association alone is not proof; objective lung-function, imaging or exposure evidence should support the diagnosis when possible.
assessment: Document every current/past job, specific tasks, agents/material safety data, ventilation/PPE, coworkers with symptoms and symptom timing during work, days off and vacations.
Ask smoking/vaping, hobbies/home exposures and nonoccupational mimics so the workplace is not assumed to be causal without evidence.
workup: For suspected work-related asthma, use quality spirometry/bronchodilator testing and serial peak-flow or specialist challenge strategies tied to work/off-work periods when appropriate.
For suspected pneumoconiosis/ILD, use imaging and PFTs plus specialist/occupational-medicine assessment.
Do not rely on an archived occupational-asthma guideline as current operational policy; use contemporary specialty and provincial occupational-health pathways.
management: Reduce/stop harmful exposure as early as feasible while avoiding unsupported advice that jeopardizes employment without a documented plan.
Coordinate respirology, occupational medicine, workplace health/safety and compensation/reporting processes according to provincial law.
Treat the resulting asthma/COPD/ILD according to the actual disease phenotype in addition to exposure control.
medicationSafety: Escalating inhalers while harmful exposure continues can mask deterioration and does not substitute for exposure control.
Respirators/PPE must be appropriate to the hazard and fit-tested where required; generic mask advice is not sufficient occupational control.
redFlags: Acute toxic inhalation with respiratory distress
Hemoptysis or malignancy concern after high-risk exposure
counselling: Explain the importance of objective documentation and early exposure control while respecting employment, income and worker-rights concerns.
Provide smoking cessation support because smoking can amplify occupational respiratory risk.
followUp: Track symptoms/lung function after exposure modification and ensure required occupational-health referrals/reporting are closed-loop.
Reassess if symptoms fail to improve away from exposure because an alternative or additional diagnosis may be present.
examTrap: Increasing asthma therapy repeatedly without asking whether symptoms occur only at work—or declaring occupational asthma from history alone without objective support.
oneLinePearl: For occupational lung disease, the work calendar is part of the diagnostic test.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current respiratory/PFT resources
Provincial occupational-health and worker-safety pathways; archived CTS occupational-asthma guideline is not treated as current
